nameStory: The Gilled Polypore gets its name from a fascinating fungal identity crisis! While most bracket fungi in its family have tiny pores on their undersides, this rebel species sports gills like a mushroom, making it the "gilled" member of the polypore group. It's also called the Birch Mazegill because it loves birch trees and its gills sometimes form maze-like patterns.
description: The Gilled Polypore is a tough, leathery bracket fungus that grows in overlapping shelves on dead hardwood trees. These fan-shaped brackets range from 1 to 5 inches wide and display beautiful concentric zones of color from cream to brown to gray. What makes this fungus special is that unlike its bracket fungus relatives, it has true gills on the underside instead of tiny pores. The whole fungus feels firm and woody, persisting on trees for months or even years.

idTips.label: Gills
idTips.description: True gills underneath instead of pores - this is the key feature! The gills are cream-colored to pale brown and sometimes form maze-like patterns where they connect.

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Fan or bracket-shaped with distinct concentric color zones ranging from white and cream at the edges to brown and gray toward the center. Surface feels smooth to slightly velvety.

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Tough and leathery when fresh, becoming hard and woody with age. You can't easily break it with your hands - it requires real force.

idTips.label: Growth Pattern
idTips.description: Grows in overlapping, shelf-like clusters directly from dead wood without a stem. Multiple brackets often emerge from the same spot.

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: Pleasant, slightly sweet or mushroomy odor when fresh, becoming nearly odorless as it ages and hardens.

habitat: Look for Gilled Polypore on dead hardwood trees throughout New England's forests, with a particular fondness for birch, maple, and oak. You'll find it in both deciduous and mixed forests, from lowland woods to mid-elevation slopes. It prefers recently dead wood and fallen logs rather than living trees.

seasonality.spring: New, fresh brackets begin emerging as temperatures warm. Look for soft, pliable specimens with bright color zones and that pleasant mushroomy smell.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season with fresh brackets appearing regularly after rains. Colors are most vibrant and gills are clearly visible on newer growth.
seasonality.fall: Continued growth on fresh specimens while older brackets become tougher. This is often the best time to find both fresh and mature examples for comparison.
seasonality.winter: Older brackets persist on trees, becoming hard and woody but still identifiable by their gilled undersides. Snow may partially conceal specimens.

funFact: This fungus is having an identity crisis at the cellular level - it evolved from ancestors with pores but somehow switched back to making gills, essentially "re-inventing" a feature that bracket fungi had abandoned millions of years ago!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with Turkey-tail, but Turkey-tail has tiny pores underneath while Gilled Polypore has obvious gills. Memory trick: "Gilled Polypore has gills you can see, Turkey-tail has pores too tiny for me!" Also distinguished from other Trametes species by the prominent gill structure rather than pores or maze-like patterns.
contextualKnowledge: This species was previously classified in a different genus (Lenzites) and you may still find it listed as Lenzites betulina in older field guides. The reclassification reflects our growing understanding of fungal relationships through DNA analysis, showing it's more closely related to other Trametes species than previously thought.
compareHints: Among its Trametes relatives, Gilled Polypore is instantly distinguished by having true gills instead of the pores found in Turkey-tail or the maze-like patterns of White Maze Polypore. While Northern Cinnabar Polypore and other relatives may show color variations, none have the distinctive gill structure that makes this species unmistakable once you know what to look for.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Turkey-tail differs from its Trametes relatives by having the most variable and vibrant color patterns - while Northern Cinnabar Polypore is distinctly reddish-orange and Hairy Bracket is notably fuzzy, turkey-tail displays the widest range of colors in distinct concentric bands.
Within the Trametes genus, this species stands out for its solid, brilliant orange color without the multicolored bands typical of Turkey-tail or the white/cream colors of many other relatives.
Unlike the smooth, velvety turkey-tail with its colorful concentric zones, lumpy bracket is much plainer and bumpier.
Unlike its Trametes relatives like turkey-tail which form flat, colorfully zoned shelves, the little nest polypore is immediately recognizable by its unique cup shape.
Among its Trametes relatives, Hairy Bracket stands out for its distinctly fuzzy upper surface - most other species in this genus like Turkey-tail and Cinnabar Bracket have smooth, almost glossy caps.

Among the turkey-tail relatives, Trametes pubescens stands out for its uniform cream coloration and velvety texture, lacking the colorful zones of turkey-tail or the bright colors of cinnabar brackets.
